side-plank-with-reach.name: Side Plank with Reach
side-plank-with-reach.execution: From a side plank with the hips high, reach the top arm up, then thread it under the torso and through, rotating the upper back, before opening it back up to the ceiling. Keep the hips high and stable throughout — only the upper body rotates. Complete reps, then switch sides.
side-plank-with-reach.why: Adds controlled thoracic rotation to the anti-lateral-flexion hold, training the obliques to both stabilize the trunk laterally and control rotation while the hips stay locked — combining frontal-plane stability with rotary control.
side-plank-with-reach.transfer: Trains the lateral and rotary core control used to stay stacked over an edge while rotating the upper body into a shot or pass; builds oblique strength for trunk rotation without losing lower-body stability.
side-plank-with-reach.cues: "Hips stay high through the reach" · "rotate the upper back" · "control the thread, don’t drop"
side-plank-with-reach.mistakes: Hips dropping during the rotation; rushing the thread; rotating from the hips instead of the t-spine
side-plank-with-reach.progression: Progress: add a light DB or pause at end range | Regress: from the knees or smaller rotation
side-plank-with-reach.muscles: Obliques, quadratus lumborum, gluteus medius, thoracic rotators

hollow-hold.name: Hollow Hold
hollow-hold.execution: Lie on your back, press the low back firmly into the floor, then lift the shoulders and legs off the ground with the arms reaching overhead, forming a shallow “dish” shape. Keep the low back glued down and the ribs pulled in. Hold the position for the prescribed time, breathing shallowly, then release.
hollow-hold.why: A maximal anti-extension isometric — the deep core works to keep the spine neutral and ribs down against the long-lever pull of the extended limbs, building whole-trunk stiffness and abdominal strength-endurance.
hollow-hold.transfer: Builds the braced, stiff trunk that transfers force between the lower and upper body during powerful skating and shooting and resists extension under contact; a foundation for force transfer and a stable core.
hollow-hold.cues: "Low back glued to the floor" · "ribs down, reach long" · "hold the dish, breathe shallow"
hollow-hold.mistakes: Low back arching (losing the dish); holding the breath; limbs too high (reducing the demand)
hollow-hold.progression: Progress: lower the limbs closer to the floor or hold longer | Regress: tuck the knees / arms by the sides
hollow-hold.muscles: Rectus abdominis, transverse abdominis, hip flexors

hollow-rock.name: Hollow Rock
hollow-rock.execution: Get into a hollow dish position (low back pressed, shoulders and legs lifted, arms overhead). Maintaining that rigid shape, rock the whole body back and forth as a unit using a small drive, without letting the dish change. Keep the low back from arching throughout. Continue for the prescribed reps or time.
hollow-rock.why: Adds dynamic movement to the hollow hold while demanding the core keep the rigid dish shape; the rocking challenges the trunk to maintain anti-extension stiffness under momentum, building robust whole-body core control.
hollow-rock.transfer: Builds the ability to keep a stiff, braced trunk while the body is moving and being jostled — relevant to maintaining force transfer and posture during dynamic skating and contact, not only in static positions.
hollow-rock.cues: "Keep the dish, rock as one piece" · "low back stays down" · "rock from the shape, not the hips"
hollow-rock.mistakes: Losing the hollow shape (arching or folding); rocking the hips/legs separately; holding the breath
hollow-rock.progression: Progress: arms fully overhead or hold a light DB | Regress: tucked hollow rock (knees bent)
hollow-rock.muscles: Rectus abdominis, transverse abdominis, hip flexors

pallof-press.name: Pallof Press
pallof-press.execution: Anchor a band at chest height to the side. Stand side-on (or half-kneeling), holding the band at the chest with both hands in an athletic stance. Press the hands straight out in front to full extension while resisting the band’s pull to rotate you toward the anchor, then return to the chest. Keep the hips and shoulders square. Reps, then switch sides.
pallof-press.why: A pure anti-rotation exercise — the band tries to rotate the trunk and the core must resist; pressing out lengthens the lever and increases the rotary challenge, building the stiffness that controls and resists trunk rotation.
pallof-press.transfer: Builds the anti-rotation core stiffness used to stay square and resist being turned in board battles and to transfer rotational force efficiently into shots and passes without leaking through the trunk.
pallof-press.cues: "Square hips and shoulders" · "press straight out, resist the twist" · "brace, control back in"
pallof-press.mistakes: Letting the torso rotate toward the anchor; pressing high or low instead of straight; holding the breath
pallof-press.progression: Progress: heavier band, step closer, or longer hold | Regress: lighter band or step farther from the anchor
pallof-press.muscles: Obliques, transverse abdominis, deep core, hip stabilizers

tall-plank-db-drag.name: Tall Plank DB Drag
tall-plank-db-drag.execution: In a high plank with the feet wide, set a DB just outside one hand. Brace hard, then reach the opposite hand across and drag the DB under the body to the other side, keeping the hips as square and level as possible. Reset and drag it back. Minimize any hip rotation or rocking throughout. Alternate.
tall-plank-db-drag.why: Dragging load across the body under a plank creates a strong anti-rotation demand — the core must resist the hips twisting as the supporting base narrows and the load shifts, building rotary trunk stiffness and shoulder stability.
tall-plank-db-drag.transfer: Trains the anti-rotation control to stay square while one arm reaches and works across the body — like reaching for a puck or fending an opponent — and the shoulder stability to support the body on one arm during contact.
tall-plank-db-drag.cues: "Hips stay square, don’t rock" · "feet wide for stability" · "slow drag, stay tight"
tall-plank-db-drag.mistakes: Hips rotating or rocking with the drag; sagging or piking; feet too narrow
tall-plank-db-drag.progression: Progress: heavier DB or feet closer | Regress: lighter DB, wider feet, or from the knees
tall-plank-db-drag.nameHint: Протяжка гантели в планке на прямых руках

bear-crawl.name: Bear Crawl
bear-crawl.execution: Start on hands and knees, knees lifted an inch off the floor (bear position), back flat, hips at shoulder height. Crawl forward by moving the opposite hand and foot together, keeping the knees low and the hips level — minimize side-to-side hip sway. Move slowly and controlled for the prescribed distance.
bear-crawl.why: Demands coordinated contralateral limb movement while the core resists rotation and keeps the spine neutral and knees hovering; builds full-body stability, anti-rotation control, and shoulder/hip coordination under a low, braced position.
bear-crawl.transfer: Trains the coordinated cross-body limb patterning and anti-rotation trunk control that underpin efficient skating mechanics, plus the shoulder/hip stability used to stay strong and balanced in low, contested positions.
bear-crawl.cues: "Knees hover low, back flat" · "hips quiet, opposite hand and foot" · "slow and stable"
bear-crawl.mistakes: Hips swaying side to side; knees rising too high; rushing and losing the brace
bear-crawl.progression: Progress: add load, crawl backward or lateral | Regress: slower, shorter distance, or knees lightly touching
bear-crawl.muscles: Anti-rotation core, shoulders, quads, hip flexors

bear-crawl-variations.name: Bear Crawl Variations
bear-crawl-variations.execution: From the bear position (knees hovering an inch off the floor, back flat, hips at shoulder height), perform crawling variations — moving laterally, backward, or adding a shoulder tap or reach between steps. Keep the knees low, hips level, and resist any twisting. Move slowly and controlled through each pattern for the prescribed distance or time.
bear-crawl-variations.why: Challenges anti-rotation core control and shoulder/hip coordination across multiple directions; varying the direction and adding reaches forces the trunk to stabilize against different rotary and shifting loads, broadening full-body stability.
bear-crawl-variations.transfer: Builds the multi-directional coordination and trunk control that transfer to the varied directional demands of skating — forward, lateral, and backward — while keeping a strong, stable core in low contested positions.
bear-crawl-variations.cues: "Knees hover, back flat" · "hips quiet in every direction" · "slow, controlled, no twist"
bear-crawl-variations.mistakes: Hips swaying or rotating; knees popping up high; rushing and losing the brace
bear-crawl-variations.progression: Progress: add load, longer distance, or harder direction patterns | Regress: forward crawl only, slower, shorter distance
bear-crawl-variations.muscles: Anti-rotation core, shoulders, quads, hip flexors

copenhagen-plank-short.name: Copenhagen Plank (Short)
copenhagen-plank-short.execution: Lie on your side with the top leg’s lower shin or knee resting on a bench, forearm under the shoulder on the floor. Lift the hips so the body forms a straight line, supported by the forearm and the bench, the bottom leg hovering or lightly assisting. Squeeze the top-leg inner thigh to hold. Hold for the prescribed time, then switch sides.
copenhagen-plank-short.why: Loads the top-leg adductors isometrically as they support the hips against gravity, while the lateral core resists side-bending; the short lever (knee/shin on bench) reduces the load, building adductor and lateral-core strength safely.
copenhagen-plank-short.transfer: Directly strengthens the adductors that power and stabilize the skating stride and resist the groin strains common in hockey; the lateral-core demand supports staying stacked over an edge.
copenhagen-plank-short.cues: "Squeeze the top inner thigh" · "hips high, body in a line" · "don’t let the hips sag"
copenhagen-plank-short.mistakes: Hips sagging toward the floor; rotating the torso; relying on the bottom leg
copenhagen-plank-short.progression: Progress: lengthen the lever (foot on bench) or add a hold/load | Regress: shorter hold or bottom leg assists more
copenhagen-plank-short.muscles: Adductors, obliques, quadratus lumborum, hip stabilizers

copenhagen-plank-long.name: Copenhagen Plank — Long
copenhagen-plank-long.execution: Lie on your side with the top leg’s foot or ankle on a bench (long lever), forearm under the shoulder. Lift the hips into a straight line, supported by the forearm and the top foot, the bottom leg lifted or hovering. Squeeze the top-leg adductor to hold. Hold for the prescribed time, keeping the body rigid, then switch sides.
copenhagen-plank-long.why: The long lever (foot on the bench) greatly increases the adductor’s isometric load as it supports the body’s weight, building high-level adductor strength and lateral-core stability — a key protective and performance quality for the groin.
copenhagen-plank-long.transfer: Builds strong, resilient adductors that drive and stabilize the skating stride and crossovers and protect against groin strains; the lateral-core stiffness supports balance over a single edge under load.
copenhagen-plank-long.cues: "Drive the top heel into the bench" · "hips high, rigid line" · "squeeze the inner thigh hard"
copenhagen-plank-long.mistakes: Hips sagging; bending at the waist; the bottom leg dropping to assist
copenhagen-plank-long.progression: Progress: add ankle weight / top-leg raises or longer hold | Regress: short-lever Copenhagen (knee on bench)
copenhagen-plank-long.muscles: Adductors, obliques, quadratus lumborum, hip stabilizers

banded-chop-lift.name: Banded Chop / Lift
banded-chop-lift.execution: Anchor a band high for a chop (or low for a lift). In a tall- or half-kneeling stance, grip the band with both hands and pull it diagonally across the body — high-to-low for a chop, low-to-high for a lift — keeping the arms relatively straight and moving from the trunk. Resist rotation; control it back. Reps each pattern and side.
banded-chop-lift.why: Trains the core to produce and resist rotation through a diagonal pattern; the trunk transfers force across the body while the deep core and obliques control the rotary load, building rotational strength and anti-rotation control together.
banded-chop-lift.transfer: Builds the diagonal trunk power and control used to transfer force into shots and passes and to stay stable while rotating; the half-kneeling base reinforces hip and core stability for these rotary actions.
banded-chop-lift.cues: "Move from the trunk, not the arms" · "stay tall, hips still" · "control the diagonal back"
banded-chop-lift.mistakes: Pulling with just the arms; the hips/torso collapsing toward the anchor; rushing the pattern
banded-chop-lift.progression: Progress: heavier band, standing, or add rotation | Regress: lighter band or smaller range
banded-chop-lift.muscles: Obliques, transverse abdominis, lats, shoulders, hip stabilizers

hanging-knee-raise.name: Hanging Knee Raise
hanging-knee-raise.execution: Hang from a pull-up bar, shoulders lightly packed, legs straight. Brace the core and raise the knees toward the chest by curling the pelvis up (posterior tilt), not just flexing the hips. Pause briefly, then lower the legs under control without swinging. Keep the movement deliberate and the grip secure. Repeat for reps.
hanging-knee-raise.why: Trains the lower abs and hip flexors through hip flexion with a pelvic curl; controlling the eccentric without swinging builds anterior-core strength and control, plus grip endurance from the hang.
hanging-knee-raise.transfer: Builds the lower-core and hip-flexor strength used in the knee-drive recovery of the stride and in maintaining a stable, braced pelvis; the grip demand supports stick control in battles.
hanging-knee-raise.cues: "Curl the pelvis, not just the hips" · "no swinging, control down" · "shoulders packed"
hanging-knee-raise.mistakes: Swinging or using momentum; only flexing the hips (no pelvic curl); dropping the legs fast
hanging-knee-raise.progression: Progress: straight-leg raise or add ankle weight | Regress: bent-knee tucks or lying leg raises

dragon-flag-negatives.name: Dragon Flag Negatives
dragon-flag-negatives.execution: Lie on a bench and grip behind your head for anchorage. Kick the legs up so the body is near-vertical, supported on the upper back, then lower the rigid, straight body slowly toward the bench as one unit, resisting the descent. Keep the whole body stiff — no bending at the hips. Reset and repeat the lowering.
dragon-flag-negatives.why: A maximal anti-extension eccentric — the entire body acts as one rigid lever lowered slowly, demanding enormous deep-core strength to keep the spine neutral against the long-lever gravitational load; builds high-level trunk stiffness and abdominal strength.
dragon-flag-negatives.transfer: Builds elite trunk rigidity that transfers force between the lower and upper body and resists extension under heavy contact; the whole-body stiffness supports powerful, leak-free force transfer in skating and shooting.
dragon-flag-negatives.cues: "One rigid line, no hip break" · "lower slow, fight gravity" · "ribs down, brace hard"
dragon-flag-negatives.mistakes: Bending at the hips (losing the rigid line); dropping too fast; arching the low back
dragon-flag-negatives.progression: Progress: slower negatives or full dragon flags | Regress: bent-knee/tucked negatives or hollow holds
dragon-flag-negatives.muscles: Rectus abdominis, transverse abdominis, hip flexors, lats

pallof-march.name: Pallof March
pallof-march.execution: Anchor a band at chest height to the side; hold it pressed out (or at the chest) and stand tall, hips and shoulders square. Maintaining the anti-rotation brace, march one knee up to hip height, lower it, then the other — resisting any rotation or side-tilt the whole time. Keep the press steady. Reps, then switch sides.
pallof-march.why: Adds a marching, single-leg-loading challenge to the Pallof anti-rotation hold; lifting each leg shifts the base of support and adds hip flexion while the core keeps resisting rotation, training rotary stability under a moving base.
pallof-march.transfer: Trains the anti-rotation core control to stay square while the legs move and load alternately — exactly the demand of skating, where the trunk must stay stable as each leg drives; supports efficient force transfer.
pallof-march.cues: "Hips and shoulders square, march tall" · "resist the twist as the knee lifts" · "steady press, steady core"
pallof-march.mistakes: Torso rotating toward the anchor as a knee lifts; tilting side to side; rushing the march
pallof-march.progression: Progress: press fully out while marching or heavier band | Regress: hold at the chest, lighter band, slower march
pallof-march.muscles: Obliques, transverse abdominis, hip flexors, deep core

hanging-straight-leg-raise.name: Hanging Straight-Leg Raise
hanging-straight-leg-raise.execution: Hang from a bar, shoulders lightly packed, legs straight. Brace and raise the straight legs toward horizontal (or higher), curling the pelvis at the top, without swinging. Pause, then lower the straight legs under control to the start. Keep the legs straight and the movement deliberate throughout. Repeat for reps.
hanging-straight-leg-raise.why: A long-lever anterior-core exercise — keeping the legs straight greatly increases the load on the lower abs and hip flexors through the raise and controlled lowering, building strong anterior-core and hip-flexor strength plus grip endurance.
hanging-straight-leg-raise.transfer: Builds the strong lower-core and hip-flexor strength used in powerful knee/leg drive and a braced pelvis during skating; the grip and core demand supports stability and stick control through battles.
hanging-straight-leg-raise.cues: "Straight legs, curl at the top" · "no swing, control the lower" · "shoulders packed, brace"
hanging-straight-leg-raise.mistakes: Swinging or kipping; bending the knees to cheat; dropping the legs uncontrolled
hanging-straight-leg-raise.progression: Progress: raise higher (toes-to-bar) or add ankle weight | Regress: hanging knee raise or bent-knee raises
hanging-straight-leg-raise.muscles: Lower abs, hip flexors, forearm/grip, lats

plank-shoulder-tap.name: Plank Shoulder Tap
plank-shoulder-tap.execution: Start in a high plank, feet about hip-width (wider is easier), body in a straight line and braced. Lift one hand to tap the opposite shoulder while keeping the hips as square and still as possible, then return and tap with the other hand. Minimize any side-to-side hip rock. Alternate taps at a controlled pace.
plank-shoulder-tap.why: Lifting one hand removes a point of support and creates an anti-rotation demand — the core must resist the hips twisting toward the unsupported side, building rotary trunk stiffness and shoulder stability in a simple, scalable drill.
plank-shoulder-tap.transfer: Builds the anti-rotation core control to stay square when weight or support shifts to one side — relevant to a stable trunk during one-arm reaches and contact — plus shoulder stability under shifting load.
plank-shoulder-tap.cues: "Hips square, don’t rock" · "feet wide for stability" · "slow, controlled taps"
plank-shoulder-tap.mistakes: Hips rocking side to side; sagging or piking; rushing the taps
plank-shoulder-tap.progression: Progress: feet closer together or add a tempo | Regress: wider feet or from the knees

bear-crawl-with-dbs.name: Bear Crawl with DBs
bear-crawl-with-dbs.execution: Set up in the bear position gripping a DB in each hand (knees hovering, back flat, hips level). Crawl forward moving the opposite hand and foot together, keeping the knees low and the hips level while the hands grip the DBs. Move slowly and controlled, resisting any twist. Continue for the prescribed distance.
bear-crawl-with-dbs.why: Adds load and an unstable gripping surface to the bear crawl, increasing the demand on the anti-rotation core, shoulder stabilizers, and grip; the DBs raise the stability challenge while the contralateral pattern builds coordination under load.
bear-crawl-with-dbs.transfer: Builds loaded full-body stability, anti-rotation control, and grip strength that transfer to staying strong and balanced in low, contested positions while controlling the stick; reinforces coordinated cross-body movement under load.
bear-crawl-with-dbs.cues: "Grip the DBs, knees low" · "hips quiet, opposite hand and foot" · "slow and stable"
bear-crawl-with-dbs.mistakes: Hips swaying or rotating; knees rising; the DBs tipping (losing wrist control)
bear-crawl-with-dbs.progression: Progress: heavier DBs or longer distance | Regress: bodyweight bear crawl
bear-crawl-with-dbs.muscles: Anti-rotation core, shoulders, quads, hip flexors, grip

plank-hold.name: Plank Hold
plank-hold.execution: Set the forearms on the floor under the shoulders, feet hip-width, and lift the body into a straight line from head to heels. Brace the core, squeeze the glutes, and pull the ribs down so the low back stays neutral. Hold for the prescribed time, breathing steadily, then lower. Don’t let the hips sag or pike.
plank-hold.why: A foundational anti-extension isometric — the deep core, glutes, and shoulders work to keep the spine neutral against gravity’s pull to sag, building whole-trunk stiffness and the postural endurance that underpins force transfer.
plank-hold.transfer: Builds the braced trunk that transfers leg and arm force without leaking through a soft midsection during skating and shooting, and resists extension under contact; a base-level core stability builder.
plank-hold.cues: "Straight line, squeeze the glutes" · "ribs down, brace" · "don’t let the hips sag"
plank-hold.mistakes: Hips sagging (low back arching) or piking up; holding the breath; shoulders not over the elbows
plank-hold.progression: Progress: add a load on the back, long-lever plank, or max-tension hold | Regress: from the knees or shorten the hold
plank-hold.muscles: Rectus abdominis, transverse abdominis, glutes, shoulders

skater-hop-stick-it.name: Skater Hop — Stick It
skater-hop-stick-it.execution: From a single-leg athletic stance, push off explosively sideways and bound onto the opposite leg, swinging the arms for momentum. Land softly on the outside leg with a bent knee and the hips back, and “stick” the landing — holding balanced for a moment before the next bound. Absorb the landing quietly. Alternate sides.
skater-hop-stick-it.why: Trains lateral (frontal-plane) power via the glutes and the stretch-shortening cycle, while the stuck landing develops eccentric deceleration strength and single-leg landing control — the ability to absorb and stabilize force.
skater-hop-stick-it.transfer: Directly mirrors the lateral push-off of the skating stride and crossovers; sticking the landing trains the deceleration and single-leg stability used to stop, change direction, and balance on an edge after a hard push.
skater-hop-stick-it.cues: "Push sideways, land soft" · "stick it, hold the landing" · "knee out, hips back"
skater-hop-stick-it.mistakes: Landing stiff or loud; knee caving inward; not holding the stick (rushing the next hop)
skater-hop-stick-it.progression: Progress: bound farther or add a hold/load | Regress: smaller bound or step between hops

jump-squat.name: Jump Squat
jump-squat.execution: Stand shoulder-width, dip into a quarter-to-half squat, then explosively extend the hips, knees, and ankles to jump straight up, swinging the arms. Land softly on the whole foot with bent knees, absorbing the impact, and reset. Keep the chest tall and the knees tracking over the toes. Repeat with full intent each rep.
jump-squat.why: Trains vertical power and rate of force development through triple extension and the stretch-shortening cycle; the explosive concentric recruits high-threshold motor units, while soft landings build eccentric absorption.
jump-squat.transfer: Develops the explosive triple extension that powers stride push-off and acceleration; the vertical force production transfers to the leg drive used to accelerate and the eccentric control used to absorb landings and stops.
jump-squat.cues: "Dip and explode up" · "full extension, reach tall" · "land soft, quiet feet"
jump-squat.mistakes: Sinking too deep or slow before jumping; knees caving; stiff or loud landings
jump-squat.progression: Progress: add load (DBs) or a continuous/contrast variation | Regress: reduce jump height or do a non-jumping squat

broad-jump.name: Broad Jump
broad-jump.execution: From an athletic stance, swing the arms back and dip the hips, then explosively extend and throw the arms forward to jump forward for maximal distance. Land softly on both feet with bent knees and the hips back, sticking the landing under control. Reset fully before the next jump. Maximize horizontal projection each rep.
broad-jump.why: Trains horizontal power and rate of force development via triple extension projected forward; the broad jump emphasizes horizontal force production (hip extension) and the stuck landing builds eccentric deceleration strength.
broad-jump.transfer: Directly mirrors the horizontal force production of skating acceleration and the explosive first strides; the forward projection trains the hip-driven push-off, and the stick trains deceleration and landing control.
broad-jump.cues: "Throw the arms, jump far" · "drive the hips forward" · "stick the landing, hips back"
broad-jump.mistakes: Jumping up instead of out; falling forward on landing (no control); not using the arm swing
broad-jump.progression: Progress: continuous/repeat broad jumps or jump-to-sprint | Regress: shorter jump or step back to reset

squat-to-tuck-jump.name: Squat to Tuck Jump
squat-to-tuck-jump.execution: From a squat, explosively jump straight up and quickly tuck both knees toward the chest at the peak, then extend the legs to land softly on the whole foot with bent knees. Absorb the landing and reset. Keep the chest tall and minimize forward lean. Repeat with quick, snappy tucks.
squat-to-tuck-jump.why: Combines explosive vertical jumping with rapid hip flexion (the tuck), training lower-body power and the speed of pulling the knees up — reinforcing fast triple extension followed by quick leg recovery, plus reactive landing control.
squat-to-tuck-jump.transfer: Builds explosive vertical power and the fast knee recovery used in stride turnover and acceleration; the quick tuck mirrors the rapid leg-recovery phase, while soft landings train deceleration control.
squat-to-tuck-jump.cues: "Explode up, snap the knees up" · "land soft and tall" · "quick tuck, quick reset"
squat-to-tuck-jump.mistakes: Leaning forward to tuck; slow or lazy tucks; stiff landings
squat-to-tuck-jump.progression: Progress: continuous tuck jumps or higher tuck | Regress: jump squat (no tuck) or reduce height

broad-jump-sprint-10m.name: Broad Jump → Sprint 10m
broad-jump-sprint-10m.execution: Perform a maximal broad jump, and on landing immediately transition into a 10-metre acceleration sprint without a pause — converting the landing into the first driving strides. Drive the arms and lean forward into the acceleration. Reset and repeat with full recovery between efforts. Emphasize a seamless jump-to-sprint transition.
broad-jump-sprint-10m.why: Links explosive horizontal jumping power directly to sprint acceleration, training the nervous system to convert a single powerful effort into continuous horizontal force production; develops the power-to-speed transfer and acceleration mechanics.
broad-jump-sprint-10m.transfer: Mirrors the explosive first push into top-speed acceleration in skating — converting an initial powerful drive into successive accelerating strides; trains the transition from standing power to building speed.
broad-jump-sprint-10m.cues: "Stick and go — no pause" · "lean and drive the arms" · "first strides powerful"
broad-jump-sprint-10m.mistakes: Pausing on landing (breaking the chain); standing too upright in the acceleration; cutting the sprint short
broad-jump-sprint-10m.progression: Progress: longer sprint or resisted start | Regress: shorter sprint or jump-then-jog
broad-jump-sprint-10m.nameHint: Прыжок в длину с места → спринт 10 м

lateral-bound-stick.name: Lateral Bound — Stick
lateral-bound-stick.execution: From a single-leg stance, push off explosively to the side and bound laterally onto the opposite leg, then stick and hold the landing on a bent knee with the hips back and balanced. Pause to fully control the landing before pushing back the other way. Absorb quietly and keep the knee tracking out. Alternate.
lateral-bound-stick.why: Develops lateral push-off power through the glutes and the stretch-shortening cycle, with strong emphasis on the eccentric deceleration and single-leg landing stability from the held stick — producing and then absorbing frontal-plane force.
lateral-bound-stick.transfer: Mirrors the lateral push and edge-loading of crossovers and the stride; the stuck landing trains the deceleration and single-leg edge control used to stop, cut, and stabilize after a hard lateral push.
lateral-bound-stick.cues: "Push hard sideways" · "stick and hold, knee out" · "land soft, hips back"
lateral-bound-stick.mistakes: Knee caving on landing; not holding the stick; landing stiff or off-balance
lateral-bound-stick.progression: Progress: bound farther or add load | Regress: smaller bound or step to reset

lateral-skater-bound.name: Lateral Skater Bound
lateral-skater-bound.execution: Bound laterally from one leg to the other in a continuous, rhythmic pattern, swinging the arms and pushing off explosively each time. Land on the outside leg with a soft, athletic knee and immediately push back the other way, minimizing ground-contact time. Keep the bounds powerful and reactive. Continue for reps or distance.
lateral-skater-bound.why: Trains reactive lateral power and the stretch-shortening cycle with short ground-contact times; the continuous rhythm develops elastic frontal-plane power and the ability to quickly reabsorb and redirect force side to side.
lateral-skater-bound.transfer: Directly mirrors the rhythmic, reactive lateral push of skating strides and crossovers; minimizing contact time trains the quick, elastic push-off and edge changes used for repeated powerful strides and agility.
lateral-skater-bound.cues: "Quick, reactive, side to side" · "soft knee, push right back" · "swing the arms with rhythm"
lateral-skater-bound.mistakes: Long, heavy ground contacts; knees caving; losing rhythm or balance
lateral-skater-bound.progression: Progress: cover more distance or add reactive cues | Regress: skater hop with a brief stick between bounds

pogo-hops.name: Pogo Hops
pogo-hops.execution: Standing tall, hop continuously straight up off both feet using mostly the ankles, with the knees nearly straight and stiff. Land on the balls of the feet and immediately rebound with the shortest possible ground contact, like a pogo stick. Keep the body tall and rigid and the rhythm quick. Continue for reps or time.
pogo-hops.why: Trains lower-leg reactive strength and the stretch-shortening cycle at the ankle — building tendon stiffness (especially the Achilles) and the fast, elastic rebound that comes from minimizing ground-contact time, the foundation of reactive power.
pogo-hops.transfer: Builds the ankle stiffness and reactive elasticity that improve push-off efficiency and quick, repeated strides; a stiff, reactive ankle transfers more force into each skating push and supports quick feet.
pogo-hops.cues: "Stiff ankles, quick feet" · "tall and rigid, minimal knee bend" · "shortest contact, bounce fast"
pogo-hops.mistakes: Bending the knees too much (turning it into a squat jump); slow, heavy contacts; collapsing posture
pogo-hops.progression: Progress: single-leg pogos or higher/faster hops | Regress: lower, slower hops or reduce reps

skater-hop-complex.name: Skater Hop Complex
skater-hop-complex.execution: Perform a programmed series of lateral skater movements in sequence — for example, a maximal bound with a stuck landing, followed by several continuous reactive bounds, then repeat. Push off explosively each time, controlling the stuck landings and minimizing contact on the continuous ones. Follow the prescribed sequence and reset between rounds.
skater-hop-complex.why: Combines maximal-effort bounds (force/power) with reactive continuous bounds (elastic, short-contact power) in one sequence, training the full spectrum of frontal-plane power — from absorbing and producing maximal force to fast reactive rebounds.
skater-hop-complex.transfer: Develops both the powerful single lateral push (hard crossover or stride) and the quick reactive repeated pushes of skating; trains combining a big push with fast follow-up strides during acceleration and agility.
skater-hop-complex.cues: "Big push, stick it — then quick and reactive" · "knees out, land soft" · "follow the sequence"
skater-hop-complex.mistakes: Knees caving; sloppy stuck landings; losing rhythm on the continuous portion
skater-hop-complex.progression: Progress: add load or more reactive reps | Regress: fewer reps or stick every landing
skater-hop-complex.muscles: Glutes, quads, adductors/abductors, calves, hip stabilizers

multi-direction-bound.name: Multi-Direction Bound
multi-direction-bound.execution: Bound explosively in varied directions on a prescribed pattern — forward, laterally, and diagonally — landing softly on one or both legs and controlling each landing before the next bound. Use the arms for momentum and keep the knees tracking out. Reset balance between directional changes. Follow the prescribed sequence.
multi-direction-bound.why: Trains power production and landing control across multiple planes (sagittal, frontal, and diagonal); varying the direction develops the multi-planar reactive strength and stability needed to produce and absorb force in any direction.
multi-direction-bound.transfer: Mirrors the multi-directional explosive demands of skating — forward acceleration, lateral crossovers, and diagonal cuts — building the power and single-leg control to push off and stabilize in whatever direction the play demands.
multi-direction-bound.cues: "Explode in each direction, land controlled" · "knees out, soft landings" · "balance before the next bound"
multi-direction-bound.mistakes: Knees caving on landing; rushing without controlling landings; losing balance between directions
multi-direction-bound.progression: Progress: faster transitions or reactive (cued) directions | Regress: fewer directions or stick each landing
multi-direction-bound.muscles: Glutes, quads, adductors/abductors, hip stabilizers, calves

ankle-hop-stick.name: Ankle Hop Stick
ankle-hop-stick.execution: From a tall stance, perform a stiff-ankle hop (mostly from the ankles, minimal knee bend), then land on the balls of the feet and stick the landing quietly under control, holding balanced. Reset and repeat. Emphasize a stiff, reactive ankle on the hop and a quiet, controlled stick on the landing.
ankle-hop-stick.why: Combines the ankle stiffness and reactive-strength stimulus of a pogo hop with a controlled stuck landing, training both the elastic ankle rebound and the ability to absorb and stabilize landing forces through the lower leg and foot.
ankle-hop-stick.transfer: Builds the stiff, reactive ankle that improves push-off efficiency in skating, plus the landing control and ankle/foot stability that support balanced edges and quick feet; reinforces force absorption through the lower leg.
ankle-hop-stick.cues: "Stiff ankle on the hop" · "stick quiet, hold it" · "tall posture, balanced"
ankle-hop-stick.mistakes: Excessive knee bend; loud or uncontrolled landing; not holding the stick
ankle-hop-stick.progression: Progress: single-leg ankle hop stick or higher hop | Regress: lower hop or two-foot landing

single-leg-pogo-hops.name: Single-Leg Pogo Hops
single-leg-pogo-hops.execution: Standing on one leg, hop continuously straight up using mostly the ankle, with the knee nearly straight and stiff. Land on the ball of the foot and immediately rebound with the shortest possible ground contact. Keep the body tall and the hips level; use the arms for balance. Continue for reps, then switch legs.
single-leg-pogo-hops.why: Trains single-leg ankle stiffness and reactive strength through the stretch-shortening cycle, building unilateral tendon stiffness (Achilles), reactive elasticity, and the single-leg stability to control repeated fast rebounds — exposing left-right differences.
single-leg-pogo-hops.transfer: Builds the single-leg ankle stiffness and reactive push that improve each skating stride’s efficiency; the unilateral demand mirrors the one-leg nature of each push and improves balance and quick, elastic feet on one edge.
single-leg-pogo-hops.cues: "Stiff ankle, hips level" · "minimal knee bend, quick contacts" · "tall and balanced"
single-leg-pogo-hops.mistakes: Too much knee bend; hips dropping to the free side; slow, heavy contacts
single-leg-pogo-hops.progression: Progress: higher/faster hops or add directional travel | Regress: two-leg pogo hops or lower height
single-leg-pogo-hops.muscles: Calves/Achilles, anterior tibialis, foot/ankle and hip stabilizers

high-low-pogo-combo.name: High-Low Pogo Combo
high-low-pogo-combo.execution: Alternate between low, fast pogo hops (small amplitude, very quick contacts) and higher pogo hops (greater amplitude) in a prescribed rhythm — for example, several quick low hops then a few high hops. Keep the ankles stiff and the body tall throughout, landing on the balls of the feet with short contacts. Follow the sequence.
high-low-pogo-combo.why: Varies the amplitude and rhythm of reactive ankle hopping, training both fast low-amplitude reactivity (quick contacts) and higher-amplitude reactive power; switching between them develops a versatile, elastic lower leg across different stiffness demands.
high-low-pogo-combo.transfer: Builds the range of ankle reactivity used in skating — from quick, short choppy strides to longer powerful pushes; the varied rhythm trains the lower leg to produce elastic force at different cadences for quick feet and efficient strides.
high-low-pogo-combo.cues: "Stiff ankles throughout" · "low and fast, then high" · "tall, short contacts"
high-low-pogo-combo.mistakes: Knees taking over (losing the ankle stiffness); mushy or long contacts; losing the rhythm sequence
high-low-pogo-combo.progression: Progress: single-leg or faster transitions | Regress: steady same-height pogos

drop-squat.name: Drop Squat
drop-squat.execution: Stand tall, then quickly drop the body down into an athletic quarter-squat landing position — feet snapping out to landing width, hips back, knees bent and tracking out — absorbing the descent and freezing in a stable, braced stance. The aim is to “beat the floor down” and stick the position instantly. Reset tall and repeat.
drop-squat.why: Trains the rate of eccentric force absorption and the speed of getting into a stable landing position; quickly dropping and stabilizing builds reactive deceleration strength and the ability to “find the floor” fast — the catching half of plyometrics.
drop-squat.transfer: Builds the rapid deceleration and stable athletic positions used to stop quickly, absorb contact, and reset on the ice; trains the catch mechanics that protect the knees on hard stops and direction changes.
drop-squat.cues: "Beat the floor down" · "snap into the stance, freeze" · "knees out, hips back, soft"
drop-squat.mistakes: Landing tall or stiff (no hip load); knees caving; slow, uncontrolled drop with no stick
drop-squat.progression: Progress: drop to a deeper/single-leg position or from a small hop | Regress: slower controlled drop to a higher position

depth-drop-low-box.name: Depth Drop (Low Box)
depth-drop-low-box.execution: Stand on a low box, step (don’t jump) off the edge, and land on both feet in an athletic position — knees bent, hips back, weight on the whole foot. Stick and hold the landing quietly under control, absorbing the impact without collapsing. Step back up and reset. Keep the landings soft and balanced.
depth-drop-low-box.why: Isolates the eccentric landing phase — dropping from height increases the impact force the legs must absorb, training eccentric strength and the reactive stiffness and joint control needed to decelerate and stabilize landing forces safely.
depth-drop-low-box.transfer: Builds the landing absorption and deceleration control used to stop hard, land from contact, and stabilize after jumps and falls; the eccentric strength protects the knees and supports quick, controlled stops on the ice.
depth-drop-low-box.cues: "Step off, don’t jump" · "land soft and quiet, stick it" · "knees out, hips back"
depth-drop-low-box.mistakes: Jumping off (adding height); landing stiff or loud; knees caving; collapsing too deep
depth-drop-low-box.progression: Progress: higher box or single-leg depth drop | Regress: lower box or step-down to a stick
depth-drop-low-box.muscles: Quads, glutes, hamstrings, calves, hip stabilizers

depth-jump-low-box.name: Depth Jump (Low Box)
depth-jump-low-box.execution: Stand on a low box, step off and land on both feet, then immediately on contact rebound into a maximal vertical jump — minimizing the time on the ground between landing and takeoff. Land softly from the rebound and reset. Treat the floor like it’s hot: land and explode up instantly.
depth-jump-low-box.why: The premier reactive-strength exercise — the drop pre-loads the muscles and tendons, and the fast ground contact uses the stretch-shortening cycle to produce a more powerful jump; trains rate of force development and the rapid switch from absorbing to producing force.
depth-jump-low-box.transfer: Builds the reactive, elastic power that lets a skater convert each ground contact into a forceful push quickly — improving explosive stride power and the rapid stretch-shortening action behind powerful acceleration and quick first steps.
depth-jump-low-box.cues: "Floor is hot — land and explode" · "shortest possible contact" · "jump up, not just off the box"
depth-jump-low-box.mistakes: Spending too long on the ground (no reactivity); jumping off the box (adding height); soft, slow rebound; sloppy landings
depth-jump-low-box.progression: Progress: higher box (within control) or single-leg | Regress: lower box or depth drop (stick only, no rebound)

banded-squat-jump.name: Banded Squat Jump
banded-squat-jump.execution: Stand on a band (or with it looped over the shoulders), feet shoulder-width. Dip into a quarter squat, then jump explosively against the band’s resistance, fighting it all the way to full extension. Land softly with bent knees, reset, and repeat. Keep the chest tall and knees tracking out, jumping with maximal intent each rep.
banded-squat-jump.why: The band adds accommodating resistance that increases through the jump, overloading the concentric phase and forcing greater force production through extension; trains explosive strength and accelerative power against rising resistance, with a faster reactive descent.
banded-squat-jump.transfer: Builds the forceful, accelerative leg extension behind a powerful stride push-off; the rising resistance trains the athlete to keep driving through full extension — mirroring the need to finish the skating push with force rather than fading.
banded-squat-jump.cues: "Fight the band to full extension" · "explode up, finish tall" · "land soft, reset"
banded-squat-jump.mistakes: Not reaching full extension (the band wins); knees caving; stiff landings; dipping too slowly
banded-squat-jump.progression: Progress: heavier band or add a hold/DB | Regress: lighter band or bodyweight squat jump
